metadata.title: An evaluation of tiered machine learning framework to predict science achievement among Singapore students
metadata.venue: 2023 International Conference on Computational Science and Computational Intelligence (CSCI)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS assessment data for Singapore students and reports an analytic sample of 4,853 eighth-grade students (2,487 boys and 2,366 girls). The paper does not describe the use of TIMSS sampling/survey weights or any replicate-weight procedure, nor does it name weight variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT) or BRR/jackknife methods. Because the analysis is a multi-model supervised classification pipeline (XGBoost, decision trees, logistic regression, SVM, Naive Bayes) with SMOTE and feature selection, the manuscript does not indicate any complex-survey-weighted estimation; thus, weighting is likely omitted or at least not documented. For replication with TIMSS microdata, analysts should apply the official TIMSS student sampling weights and appropriate replicate weights when available, and ensure that SMOTE/feature selection are performed within resampling folds to respect the complex design.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is converted into five achievement classes using percentile cut points (≥90th, 80–90, 70–80, 60–70, ≤60), and the paper does not report using TIMSS plausible values (PV-based continuous achievement scores) in the modeling stage. Because the outcome is treated as a categorical class label rather than a PV-based cognitive score, PV handling is not applicable. Separately, the manuscript does not describe any missing-data strategy (e.g., complete-case selection or imputation), which is a reporting gap given that questionnaire-based non-cognitive predictors typically contain missing responses.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The paper uses TIMSS science assessment data for Singapore eighth-grade students and reports the participating sample as 2,487 boys and 2,366 girls (total 4,853). No additional inclusion/exclusion rules are described for constructing the analytic dataset (e.g., no stated restrictions to specific schools, modules, or complete-case criteria), and no missing-data handling procedure is reported.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Best model (XGBoost): Accuracy 57.47%, Precision 29%, Recall 27%, F1-score 27%; also reports MAE 0.99 (lowest among models).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Science (Singapore) the study leveraged socioeconomic status of parents, confidence in science, and valuing science to predict science achievement class, finding that XGBoost achieved the highest accuracy (57.47%) and precision (29%) with the lowest MAE (0.99) among the evaluated classifiers. This indicates that strengthening family socioeconomic supports and science-related student beliefs (confidence and valuing) may improve the likelihood of students being classified into higher science achievement categories, though the results are predictive and not causal and the paper does not document missing-data handling or survey-weight use.

data.outcome_summary: The study evaluates a tiered machine learning framework on TIMSS science data for Singapore eighth-grade students (N=4,853) by converting continuous science achievement into five percentile-based classes: excellent, very good, average, below average, and unsatisfactory. The framework uses SMOTE to address class imbalance, a feature-selection council to select the top three predictors, and a suite of classifiers (XGBoost, decision tree, logistic regression, SVM, Naive Bayes) with a combiner that chooses models based on accuracy/precision/recall/F1 and user preference. Across models, XGBoost performs best with Accuracy=57.47%, Precision=29%, Recall=27%, F1=27%, and the lowest MAE=0.99, while Naive Bayes is lowest (Accuracy=46.14%, MAE=1.25). The paper reports moderate correlations between predictors and the outcome and frames performance as “over 50%” accuracy, but it does not document missing-data handling or whether TIMSS sampling/replicate weights were applied, limiting generalizability and interpretability.
